In many ways, the art of making a great miniseries is to leave the audience wanting more. The art of securing a lasting legacy for a miniseries can reside in resistance, as fans and critics alike call for more despite the story running its course. Of course, not every limited series made has shown such resolve, and it has resulted in many shows that thrived with their first, self-contained season only to lose the plot as they try to expand the narrative.

The creators of the miniseries that don’t cave in to such external pressure and fanfare deserve commendation for their conviction in their storytelling triumphing over the lure of more audience engagement and, presumably, more money. Not only an admirable showing of artistic integrity, but such resolve has also established many of the greatest feats the medium has ever seen, with everything from gripping war drama to superhero suspense, romantic tragedy, and absorbing crime mystery included among the miniseries that are made better by not having ensuing seasons.

blocks.c: Colin Farrell as Oz Cobb in 'The Penguin'

blocks.x: As both a concentrated, isolated story of criminal ambition and a gripping and complex expansion on the world of Matt Reeves’ The Batman, HBO’s The Penguin soars as one of the most captivating miniseries of the decade so far. Set amid the chaos, destruction, and disorder following the events of The Batman, the eight-part limited series focuses on organized crime enforcer Oswald Cobb (Colin Farrell) as he rises to become the kingpin of crime in Gotham City.

By tracking the story through to Cobb’s acquisition of power, and by virtue of the character’s storied criminal empire in the “Batman” comic books, it would have been incredibly easy to cave to the temptation to make The Penguin an ongoing series. However, with the finale ending on the perfect note to reaffirm Cobb’s ruthless amorality and callous inhumanity, the miniseries alone delivers the perfect spin-off to The Batman as it darkens the story world of the movie, but it also serves as a faultless character study of criminal ambition, power, violence, and want.

Marianne and Connell from Normal People hugging

blocks.x: An enrapturing portrait of the magic and angst of young love, Normal People delivers a ravishing teen romance bolstered by the infectious chemistry between stars Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones. The 12-part miniseries follows the two lovers as their secretive high school relationship grows strained as they both try to decide what they want to do in life and begin to realize they may have to decide between their aspirations and their romance.

Mature, grounded, and completely empathetic to both parties, Normal People balances the tragedy and heartbreak of first love with a sense of illuminating vulnerability that extends humanity to both characters’ plights. Despite the series serving as an adaptation of Sally Rooney’s novel, the desire for a second season was abundant, and it even came to a boiling point when Mescal and Edgar-Jones’ cryptic advertisement for a charity event was misconstrued as being a teasing hint at a follow-up season. While the stars and director Lenny Abrahamson have expressed interest in returning to the story in the future, the series in isolation stands as a beautiful, all-encompassing immersion in the fragility and volatility of teenage romance.

blocks.c: Hamish Linklater in priestly garb as Father Paul in Midnight Mass.

blocks.x: Over the course of the past decade, Mike Flanagan has established himself as a spearhead of modern horror television through several acclaimed miniseries productions with Netflix. While many of his projects have been adaptations, and therefore contained to a degree by the breadth of the source material’s story, Midnight Mass could have evolved into anything as it marked Flanagan’s first original narrative in the form.

Furthermore, the story could easily have been extended into a multi-series plotline as it unfolds in a small island town as the arrival of a new priest brings much-needed miracles, but gives rise to a ghoulish horror by night as well. Its seven-episode arc proves to be perfect, though, not only because it enables the story to run with a concentrated beginning, middle, and end, but because it allows for a focused thematic exploration of faith, forgiveness, and mortality as well. There are many who herald Midnight Mass as being one of the greatest TV productions of the past decade, and while Mike Flanagan himself toyed with a second season, the standalone miniseries imbued the show with integrity and impact.

blocks.x: Sometimes when something is so outrageously good, viewers can’t help but want more, even if continuing the story doesn’t make sense. Faultless as an immersive and accurate historical drama, a heart-stopping thriller, and a poignant, timeless examination of political corruption, Chernobyl had many fans begging for any form of expansion on the five-episode run. Series creator Craig Mazin was quick to take to social media to shut down any speculation of a second season, though he did note HBO’s interest in making an anthology of sorts exploring other distinct global catastrophes. He ultimately chose not to pursue the idea, and as a result, Chernobyl endures as an incredibly rare triumph of miniseries drama in that it is almost universally heralded as being perfect.

Of course, it stands as arguably the greatest miniseries of all time and a defining pillar of the medium’s ascent to being a prestige form of drama, but the brilliance in it not having a second season is that, ironically, it actually kind of does.

The releases of 2010’s The Pacific and the 2024’s Masters of the Air both gained a lot of traction by being marketed as companion pieces to Band of Brothers. The incredibly loose approach to expanding on the original miniseries is truly ingenious, as it allows the two successors to immediately appeal to audiences while still permitting Band of Brothers to stand as its own, untouched production which, in isolation, is nothing short of a masterpiece of TV drama that could be the greatest WWII story ever produced in America.

blocks.c: Cops with yellow masks up to their noses, forming a line, brandishing clubs in Watchmen.

blocks.x: In the modern age of superhero saturation that sees franchises ignited from one-off movies, HBO’s Watchmen stands as something of a rarity. A bold expansion on Alan Moore’s acclaimed graphic novel of the same name, it unfolds in contemporary America where vigilantism has been outlawed. Following an attack on the Tulsa Police Department, cops are permitted to conceal their identities, leading Detective Angela Abar (Regina King) to adopt the moniker Sister Night as she fights against racism and investigates the decades-long legacy of crime-fighting superheroes.

Interestingly, Watchmen proved to be polarizing on release, with many admiring it as a courageous new chapter while others dismissed it completely. It wasn’t long before the miniseries’ fans, both audiences and critics, were calling for a second season, but creator Damon Lindelof reiterated that he designed the show to run as a tight, nine-episode story that he was satisfied with. The end result is a piercing drama that has aged eerily well, a commanding standout in the wheelhouse of superhero entertainment in recent years, and one of the most daring and compelling miniseries ever made.

Everything from 13 Reasons Why to Prison Break springs to mind, and Mare of Easttown could conceivably have joined their ranks had it indulged in fan outcry for a Season 2. Its seven-episode arc revels in a confronting atmosphere of hardship, despair, and real American agony, following Mare (Kate Winslet) as she investigates the murder of a teenage mother while struggling to keep her own family life from completely collapsing.

The miniseries is relentlessly bleak, be it in the horrific details of the case, Mare’s complex backstory of faded dreams, or just the dilapidated misery of Easttown as a community. However, through its narrative precision and the inherent intrigue of a miniseries mystery—the format promises an immediate resolution—Mare of Easttown is absorbing and compelling rather than merely depressing. Follow-up seasons would struggle to re-capture that delicate balance of brutal realism and slow-burning momentum, but as a succinct, rounded limited series, it delivers an impactful and cohesive crime tale that never dilutes the gravitas of its story, setting, or characters.

In staying with Wright’s written experiences, the miniseries is defined by a sense of fly-on-the-wall realism that could easily have been lost in ensuing seasons.

The gripping intrigue of Generation Kill is Wright’s emphasis on the mundane, the turmoil soldiers experience due to errors in communication, due process, and bureaucratic red tape, and the agonizing, boring inertia between action. It is unlike any other war drama seen in television or film, a piercing exposé on the inertia and incompetence of modern warfare that would have stood only to lessen its eye-opening impact had it extended beyond its seven-episode run.

Meticulously crafted from beginning to end, The Queen’s Gambit follows chess prodigy Beth Harmon (Anya Taylor-Joy) from her introduction to the game in an orphanage in 1950s Kentucky, through her battles with mental health and addiction as she rises up the ranks, and to her eventual championship tilt at a major international chess tournament in Moscow. Powered by Taylor-Joy’s stunning performance, immersive period production value, and its absorbing storytelling and pacing, The Queen’s Gambit is a masterclass in modern television that is perfect as it stands.

The primary reason for this is its comfort and confidence in delivering an open-ended conclusion that could easily have been extrapolated on, even as it resolves the adaptation of Emily St. John Mandel’s source material. The 10-part limited series unfolds 20 years after a flu virus decimates mankind, but its story of a group of traveling actors inspires optimism and hope rather than apocalyptic despair.

It is certainly a unique outlook on the end of days, and one that many viewers found to be entirely captivating and refreshing, especially as its story flashes between the devastated, collapsed civilization and the initial outbreak of the virus. The control series creator, Patrick Somerville, displays by keeping Station Eleven a taut narrative that still has inflections of impressionable, thought-provoking ambiguity is astounding, and it makes for what is one of the best and most underappreciated miniseries of all time.
